newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Big stake in Russian oil firm Yukos up for sale.
newsitem.headline: Big stake in Russian oil firm Yukos up for sale.

text.p: Russia's Bank Menatep has decided to auction a one-third stake in the country's second biggest oil group, NK Yukos, the first time shares acquired under the controversial shares-for-loans scheme have been sold off.

The 33.3 percent stake in Yukos, which has massive oil reserves, will be sold in one lot in an investment tender next month. The starting price is $160 million and the winner must invest $200 million in Yukos over two years.
Menatep-backed ZAO Laguna acquired the stake, originally 45 percent but diluted by a rights issue last month, in exchange for a $159 million loan to the government last December.

"Our decision to sell this stake is mainly tied to the fact that we have already achieved a high level of integration. This stake is to a great extent no longer useful to us," said Menatep Group press secretary Natalya Mandrova.
The decision to sell a single consolidated stake means foreigners, who may not hold more than 15 percent of Russian oil companies, are effectively barred from taking part.
Rosprom, which unites Menatep's industrial holdings, holds a 52 percent controlling stake in Yukos, whose main operating unit is Yuganskneftegaz.

Laguna won an investment tender for 33 percent of Yukos and acquired a further seven percent in a cash auction in May. In last month's rights issue, which raised Yukos's authorised capital by 26 percent, a company representing Rosprom acquired nearly 13 percent.

Winners of the shares-for-loans auctions, in which state-owned stakes in top companies were tendered in exchange for loans to the government late last year, have been able to sell them since September 1 but none has so far.
Once the original loan is repaid, auction winners keep 30 percent fo the proceeds and 70 percent goes to the government.
"We don't want to hide the fact that we are selling this stake with the aim of attracting money," said Mandrova.

The shares-for-loans scheme, masterminded by former economic reform chief Anatoly Chubais, proved highly controversial. Auction winners were often close to auction organisers and winning bids were frequently barely above the starting price.
Mandrova said the proceeds would be re-invested in Yukos, one of a dozen vertically-integrated Russian oil companies created over the last few years.
However, the company owes 351.3 billion roubles in back wages and around four trillion roubles in taxes and some of the money would be used to settle debts.

"Menatep has viewed the debts as a big problem and they know they have got to pump money into Yukos to clean up the balance sheet and I think that is the main reason they did the rights offer," said Renaissance Capital energy analyst James Bunch.
"If they sell the 33 percent, they still have voting control but it is a way for them to make some money. But it doesn't look like they are going to make a whole lot on it," he added.
With reported reserves of 11.4 billion barrels of oil, Yukos is second only to Sibneft in Russia. But Russian oil companies trade at massive discounts to their Western counterparts.

The investment tender starting price would value Yukos at $480 million. In a recent report on the oil sector, Renaissance adjusted reported reserves downwards by 35 percent to approximate to Western standards. This would still value Yukos at about six cents a reported barrel.
U.S. major Exxon Corp was valued at close to $8 a barrel.
Yuganskneftegaz shares closed on the Russian Trading System at $10.10 each on Wednesday, compared with $9.73 on Tuesday.
